title: While the World Pushes Immigrants Away, Spain Invites Half a Million
dek: Pedro Sánchez is Defying Global Political Trends, and it is Working
author: Yann Grechez Elkoubi
hero_caption: Pedro Sánchez during his appearance at Ferraz following the PSOE executive committee meeting.
body:
In January, Spain’s governing coalition announced they had passed a motion to regularize over 500,000 undocumented migrants. The rules are simple: if you have spent 5 uninterrupted months in Spain before 2026, you do not hold a criminal record, and you do not currently hold any administrative status, you are allowed to obtain a legal residency and work authorization permit. 

However, the response to this policy has not been so simple. A wide variety of political actors, ranging from Spain’s conservative opposition to the White House, have expressed complete outrage. People like Elon Musk have even called it an act of “high treason” towards the Spanish people.

Why has a domestic law of a middle power like Spain flooded news outlets across the entire globe? What are the economic and social implications of this mass regularization? Does Sánchez benefit politically from swimming against the right-wing populist tide currently sweeping international politics?

The justification for this policy was twofold: a social dimension concerning the basic rights of undocumented persons, and an economic one respecting the labor shortage Spain is currently experiencing.

sections.alt: After making his way in 2016 from Senegal to the agricultural belt of southern Spain, Mbaye Tune settled into regular seasonal work on tangerine and other fruit farms.

sections.body:
Socially, undocumented migrants in Spain have long dealt with intense labor exploitation. Those who are able to safely complete the journey from their home countries and find a job often encounter deplorable working conditions: long hours, scorching heat, no health insurance, and pay far below minimum wage. Labor rights that are supposed to defend people against this kind of exploitation fail to apply to undocumented individuals, simply because the law doesn’t protect those who are not registered under it.

Mass regularization is intended to provide legal visibility to previously invisible people, affording them the rights and conditions every worker in Spain usually enjoys. Studies have already shown that heat-related hospitalizations for workers have declined in provinces with greater exposure to the mass regularization policy, showing that it does indeed make people safer.

Economically, Spain’s low birth rates and ageing population (with an exceptionally high life expectancy) are putting the country at what experts call “a demographic crossroads”. Simply put, there are not enough active workers in the labor market to sustain the country’s historically generous welfare state (pensions, healthcare, public services).

Elma Saiz, Sánchez’s migration minister, has stated that Spain must register 250,000 foreign workers per year in order to sustain the welfare state at its current rate; hence this mass regularization program, which intends to provide documents to 300,000 migrants per year, for the next three years. Regularization also means paying taxes and contributing to social security, continuing the net positive contribution of immigrants in Spain’s economy and ultimately mitigating its demographic challenge.

Much of Spain’s unemployment is structural: unemployed Spanish workers are not able or willing to work where labor is most needed. Many labor shortages concentrate in sectors like agriculture, elder-care, domestic work, and construction, which tend to be physically demanding, seasonal, and poorly paid. Migrants make up for this shortage, as evidenced by 71% of domestic service workers, 45% of hospitality workers, 32% of construction workers, and 31% of agricultural workers being foreign.
